findings.title: [F1] Unauthenticated exposure of full user objects via GET /rest/memories (password hash, totpSecret, deluxeToken, lastLoginIp, email, role)
findings.analysis: GET /rest/memories (no Authorization) returns 200 with all stored memories, each carrying a full embedded User object. User objects expose email, a 32-hex password hash, role, a 40-hex deluxeToken, totpSecret, and lastLoginIp. Verified this boot: 200 / 6183 B / 10 records; user fields: createdAt, deletedAt, deluxeToken, email, id, isActive, lastLoginIp, password, profileImage, role, totpSecret, updatedAt, username. A bogus Bearer token produces a byte-identical 6183 B response, proving the route performs no authorization check. Controls (rest/basket, whoami, user/authentication-details, api/SecurityAnswers/) return 401. The 40-hex deluxeToken is not a signed JWT (auth attempts yield 'Invalid signature' / 'no header in signature'), so it has no hijack value on its own — but the exposure stands: every user's password hash and TOTP secret is readable by any caller without credentials, enabling offline hash cracking and TOTP-compromise, broader than a logged-in user's data. Maps to sensitive-data-exposure / password-hash-leak class.
findings.false_positive_check: Route returns the same 10-record response with no auth and with an obviously invalid Bearer token (byte-identical, md5-stable across repeats); truly gated routes return 401. The deluxeToken caveat limits account-takeover value but does not reduce the exposure (hash + TOTP secret leak regardless). User objects are never needed to render a memory listing (caption + image path suffice), so this is not a benign display requirement. Not a session-local echo: the response is returned by the same unauthenticated route each time.

findings.title: [F2] /api/SecurityAnswers/: read-gated but unauthenticated write-open gap (broken access control / no ownership validation)
findings.analysis: GET /api/SecurityAnswers/ (no Authorization) is gated (this boot returns 401-equivalent HTML 'UnauthorizedError', drifting from the earlier JSON 401 on the same campaign). POST /api/SecurityAnswers/ with no credentials and an empty body returns 201 and creates a new SecurityAnswer server-side with a server-generated id that increments across fresh requests: verified 24 -> 25 -> 26 -> 28 on this boot, UserId=null, SecurityQuestionId=null, answer=null. A populated empty-cred POST {} also returns 201 (id 27) with the answer server-side hashed, proving the write is accepted and persisted with no question-answer binding and no ownership check. The read path is protected while the write path accepts unauthenticated writes with no input validation (null answer accepted). Neighbors gated: GET /api/Complaints/, /Cards/ -> 401; /Addresses/, /Reviews/, /Questions/, /Memberships/ -> 500 'Unexpected path'. Severity: unauthenticated injection of security-answer records (null UserId) — data-integrity failure and potential security-answer poisoning / privilege-escalation vector.
findings.false_positive_check: GET consistently gated (401/HTML-unauthorized); POST consistently 201 with a fresh server id; the id sequence increments across independent fresh requests (24 -> 25 -> 26 -> 28) proving real, server-side, persistent writes rather than a local echo or validation error. Posting to a read-gated write resource without credentials should 401/403; accepting it is an authorization misconfiguration, not benign API design.

findings.title: [F5] /rest/user/security-question?email= unauthenticated account enumeration and security-question disclosure (mutation-fragile: verified 200 on this boot)
findings.analysis: GET /rest/user/security-question?email=<addr> returns 200 for both existing and nonexistent emails, but the body discriminates: configured users return {"question":{"id":N,"question":"<text>","createdAt":...,"updatedAt":...}} while nonexistent addresses return exactly 200 / 2 B '{}'. Verified this boot: bjoern@owasp.org -> {"question":{"id":7,"question":"Name of your favorite pet?",...}}; nonexistent@x.y -> 200 / '{}'. Severity: unauthenticated account-existence enumeration combined with disclosure of the account's security-question text, enabling targeted social-engineering / answer-guessing against real accounts.
findings.false_positive_check: Differential verified on both branches on the same boot: existing user returns full question JSON; nonexistent returns exactly 2 B '{}'. Neighbors gated (rest/user/authentication-details 401, other /rest/user/* 500). Not benign: the endpoint exists to look up an answer for an account the caller already owns; arbitrary callers obtaining question text + existence is information disclosure. Note: the route is mutation-fragile — 500 wrapped across boots A9/A10/A13, but 200 on A12 and this boot (A14); this submission includes it only because it reproduces 200 in the current live request set.

findings.title: [F6] Unauthenticated PUT on /api/Products/{id} persists product-tampering across requests (broken object-level authorization / HTTP-method auth gap)
findings.analysis: PUT /api/Products/{id} with no Authorization returns 200 'success' and persists arbitrary product-field modification server-side. Verified this boot: PUT {"name":"P","price":1} -> 200 with modified fields; in a subsequent fresh request, PUT {"price":1.99} (name untouched) returned the modified name 'P' — proving cross-request persistence (the prior write survived between separate requests). POST and DELETE on the same route return 401, confirming the authorization gap is specific to the PUT method (HTTP-method-level broken access control). After verification the product was restored to its original name/price. Severity: any caller can modify any product's listing (name, description, price) without credentials.
findings.false_positive_check: Cross-request persistence confirmed: a modification written in request A is observable in request B, which did not re-issue A's mutation (it only reset price) — the name field persisted. Same route with POST/DELETE -> 401, so the vulnerability is an authorization gap on the PUT update method, not global route exposure. The modification disappears only when the ephemeral benchmark DB resets; within a boot it is persistent.

findings.title: [F7] Cleartext CAPTCHA-answer leak via GET /rest/captcha (verified answer; POST submission path broken in this mutation — partial finding)
findings.analysis: GET /rest/captcha returns JSON containing the server-generated CAPTCHA expression AND its cleartext answer, e.g. {"captchaId":0,"captcha":"6-5+9","answer":"10"} (6-5+9=10) and {"captchaId":1,"captcha":"8*6-3","answer":"45"} (8*6-3=45). The answer is verifiably correct arithmetic on every instance. Severity: the correct answer is served to every unauthenticated caller, defeating the CAPTCHA entirely. This boot's POST /api/Feedbacks/ submission path rejects even the correct answer ('Wrong answer to CAPTCHA', 401) — the full bypass path is broken in this mutation — so this finding claims only the verified cleartext answer-leak vector, not the full bypass.
findings.false_positive_check: Each answer independently verified against the expression arithmetic across multiple instances on this boot (6-5+9=10; 8*6-3=45). The cleartext is returned on every GET regardless of the submission path; the broken POST path is orthogonal to (and does not explain) the GET leak. Submitted strictly as the answer-leak vector; the full bypass is not claimed because correct answers are rejected at POST.
